title: Katie Braun
text:
I got to visit the top of the world this summer!






   



Our trip to Utqiagvik involved a lot of ponds and a lot of ice wedges. We spent quite a bit of time hiking (slogging) through the tundra, an activity Christian compared to take a horizontal stairmaster. The pain was worth it, though, to get up close with a bunch of potential study sites and just spend some time thinking on the tundra.
I’ve since spent the year getting all of our drone data processed and prepared as training data for a machine learning model that I’m building to identify ice wedge degradation.

title: Katie Braun
text:
2022 Prudhoe Bay Fieldwork






   



My first trip to the Arctic packed a lot into just three days. I was originally supposed to travel with the rest of the team from Fairbanks up the Dalton Highway, but unfortunately I got COVID right before our trip and had to meet them two weeks later in Prudhoe Bay for the last leg of the trip.
At least flying over the North Slope provided some incredible views (not pictured here because I’m a terrible plane photographer).
We had three days stationed out of the Oil Field Hotel to survey degrading ice wedges, and we managed to collect enough data that I’m still not done with it, nearly two years and a full master’s thesis later.

Hello, I’m Katie!
I want to better understand how climate change is altering the surface of our planet and, in turn, how those changing landscapes impact carbon cycling. I’ve worked in a variety of landscapes, from the shoreline of the Great Lakes to the thawing permafrost of the far North. When I’m not in the field or the lab, I’m almost certainly hanging out with my cat, Louise.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions, want to chat, or would like to discuss potential projects.

title: Research Projects
text:
NASA FINESST: Mapping Thawing Permafrost
We know that the Arctic is warming over four times faster than the rest of the world, and with this warming permafrost thaws. This thaw, however, is not progressing evenly across space or time. For this project, I am using machine learning to improve our maps of thawing permafrost in ice-wedge landscapes, then use those maps to examine how ice-wedges degrade across space and time.
You can find my FINESST abstract here. Scroll down!

title: Research
text:
Research
The surface of our planet is constantly changing, sometimes in an instant - after a flood, a landslide, a wildfire, or bulldozing - sometimes so slowly the change is imperceptible to human eyes until we use some other method to detect change. As the physical world shifts around us, the living world shifts as well. Microbial communities reassemble in response to changing environmental conditions, plants colonize and compete with each other for resources, animals search for dwindling habitat patches, and humans must adapt to these impacts.
Energy and matter are constantly moving across the surface of the earth, between reservoirs in the soil, in living biomass, in the atmosphere, in a delicate dance that climate change is increasingly disrupting. The increased input of carbon into the atmosphere through altered biogeochemical cycling is a major positive feedback to climate change.
I take an earth systems approach to addressing a range of questions at the nexus of geomorphology and ecology: How are geomorphic processes responding to changing climatic conditions? How do those changing abiotic conditions influence carbon cycling? What will a certain landscape look like in ten, fifty, a hundred or a thousand years from now?
In the Arctic and beyond, I combine process-based examinations of changing earth surface dynamics and carbon cycling with remote sensing and geospatial analysis – this combination allows me to extend discrete field observations to broader landscape, regional, and global scales so we can better examine how climate change is altering our planet.
